add-to-home-screen-not-showing.html.text:
← Back to PWA Installability Checker

“Add to Home Screen” not showing? Here’s the checklist Chrome actually runs

The manifest looks right. You’ve read it three times. Chrome still won’t offer to install the page, and — this is the part that costs the hour — it never says why. The install prompt (beforeinstallprompt, and the install icon in the omnibox) is withheld silently whenever any one of five documented criteria fails. No console warning by default, no network error, nothing in the Elements panel.

This is the checklist Chrome evaluates, in order, with the failure each step actually looks like in practice — not just what the spec says should be true.

See the real reason first, before guessing

Open Chrome DevTools on the page in question, go to Application → Manifest, and look under “Installability”. Chrome lists the specific criterion it failed there, even though it never surfaces it anywhere a user or a CI log would see. That panel and the checklist on this page check the same five criteria; the difference is that DevTools needs the page open in a real Chrome window, and this tool works from a CLI fetch (usable in CI, against a staging URL, or against a page you can’t easily open in a browser).

The five criteria, in the order that catches people

#CriterionWhat it looks like when it silently fails
1A <link rel="manifest"> tag exists on this page The manifest is linked from the homepage but not from the page the visitor actually landed on — a blog post, a pricing page reached from search.
2The manifest URL returns valid JSON A trailing comma or a build step that emits the file with a wrong Content-Type so some fetchers refuse to parse it.
3name or short_name is set Rare on its own, but shows up in a hand-trimmed manifest that dropped both while removing other fields.
4display is standalone, fullscreen, or minimal-ui The most common cause. The field is left out entirely, which the spec defaults to "browser" — and "browser" is explicitly excluded from what Chrome will install. The manifest reads as complete because nothing is wrong, only absent.
5An icon of at least 192×192 (or sizes: "any") actually loads The second most common cause. The manifest lists the icon path correctly, but the file 404s (moved during a deploy, wrong build output directory) or the sizes attribute says 192x192 while the actual image file is smaller. Reading the manifest JSON alone cannot catch either — the file has to be fetched.

Why #4 and #5 are the ones that waste an hour: both pass a glance at the manifest file. The field is either present-but-wrong (an icon path that 404s) or silently defaulted (a missing display), so scanning the JSON by eye finds nothing to fix. Both require actually fetching what the manifest points at — which is what the CLI on this page does, and what reading the file in an editor cannot.

Two notices that do not block the prompt, and one thing that isn’t on this list

A missing 512×512 icon, a missing start_url, and missing theme_color/background_color are real gaps — they affect the splash screen and richer install UI — but none of them withholds the install prompt on their own. If the checklist above is clean and the prompt still doesn’t appear, these are not the cause.

A service worker is not on this checklist because it is not part of Chrome’s current installability criteria. It used to be, in older Chrome versions and in some other browsers’ implementations, so if your target is one of those, verify the prompt directly in that browser — a manifest-only check like this one has no way to see it.

If the checklist is clean and it still won’t prompt

Chrome debounces beforeinstallprompt per origin as an anti-annoyance measure: once a visitor dismisses it, or after enough visits without installing, Chrome stops firing the event for a while. Test in a fresh profile or an Incognito window before concluding the manifest is still at fault — a clean report from this checklist and a suppressed prompt from engagement heuristics look identical from the manifest’s side.

Check yours

node ventures/pwa-installability-check/check.mjs https://example.com/ --json

Paste the output into the report viewer for a plain-English breakdown of exactly which of the five criteria failed, or read the exit code directly (0 installable by this checklist, 1 otherwise) to use it as a CI gate against a regression.

Common questions

Why does Chrome not tell me why Add to Home Screen isn't showing?

Chrome evaluates the manifest silently and simply withholds the beforeinstallprompt event and the omnibox install icon when any criterion fails — there is no console error or warning by default. The one built-in way to see the reason is DevTools' Application panel, under Manifest, which lists "Installability" errors when you open it on the page in question.

My manifest looks correct. What usually causes this anyway?

The two most common causes are a display mode that defaults to "browser" because the display field was left out entirely, and an icon that is listed in the manifest but 404s or is smaller than 192x192 when actually fetched — both invisible from reading the manifest file itself, because the file can look complete while the field is absent or the icon file is missing on disk.

Does the manifest have to be linked from every page, or just the homepage?

Only the page a visitor is on needs the <link rel="manifest"> tag for Chrome to evaluate installability on that page. A manifest linked only from the homepage means a visitor who lands on an inner page first, from a search result or a shared link, gets no install prompt at all on that page even though the site is installable elsewhere.

I fixed the manifest and it still won't install. What else blocks it?

Chrome also debounces the prompt per origin: once a visitor dismisses beforeinstallprompt or after enough page visits without installing, Chrome stops firing it for a while as an anti-annoyance measure. If every documented criterion checks out and it still will not prompt on a fresh profile or an incognito window, that engagement heuristic — not the manifest — is the remaining suspect.

Do I need a service worker for the install prompt to appear?

Not for Chrome's current installability criteria, which this checklist covers in full. Some other browsers and some older Chrome versions did require a registered service worker with a fetch handler. If a specific target browser still enforces that, it will not show up in a manifest-only check like this one — verify the actual prompt in that browser directly.

index.html.text:
PWA Installability Checker

Fetches a page you choose, finds its <link rel="manifest">, fetches and parses that Web App Manifest, and fetches every icon it lists -- then classifies the result against Chrome's installability criteria: a manifest that parses, a name, an installable display mode, a secure origin, and a reachable icon of at least 192x192. These are the same checks Lighthouse's installable-manifest audit runs, with no Chrome or Puppeteer required.

1. Run the CLI against your page

Node.js 18+, no dependencies to install:

node check.mjs https://example.com/ --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass, the manifest that page links to, and the icons that manifest lists; nothing goes through this site.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Common questions

What does "installable" actually mean?

Chrome (and other browsers that support the Web App Manifest spec) will only offer to install a page as an app -- an icon on the home screen or app list, opening in its own window -- when the page's manifest clears a specific, documented checklist: a manifest exists and parses, it names the app, it declares an installable display mode, the page is served securely, and it lists a large-enough icon that actually loads. This tool runs exactly that checklist.

Why does this need a CLI instead of just checking a URL I type into the page?

This page is hosted on its own domain, and asking it to fetch an arbitrary third-party page and manifest from inside your browser is a cross-origin request -- one that fails unless that other site's server opts in with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, which almost none do for their HTML page or manifest.json. Only a non-browser HTTP client, like the CLI here (or curl, or Lighthouse's own Chrome instance), can fetch those directly. Run the CLI, then paste its JSON output here for a rendered report.

Is this the same as running Lighthouse?

It checks the same criteria as Lighthouse's installable-manifest audit -- manifest present, name, display mode, icons, secure origin -- derived from the same published Chrome documentation. It is not a full Lighthouse run: Lighthouse also scores performance, accessibility, SEO, and several other PWA checks (like an offline-capable service worker) that this tool does not attempt. Use this when you want the manifest-installability answer without installing Chrome or Puppeteer.

Does a clean report mean my app installs correctly?

It means the manifest and icons this tool could reach clear Chrome's documented installability criteria. It does not run a service worker, does not test the actual install prompt in a real browser, and cannot see a manifest field browsers might add criteria around in the future. Treat a clean report as evidence about these specific, named checks -- not a guarantee every browser will prompt to install.

Why does a missing "display" field count as a failure?

The Web App Manifest spec's default for a missing "display" is "browser" -- and Chrome's installability criteria explicitly exclude "browser" from the modes it will install. So an absent field is not neutral here; it resolves to the one value that fails the check, the same way this tool (and Lighthouse) reads it.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks the manifest fields, display mode, secure origin, and icon reachability behind Chrome's documented installability criteria. It is not a full Lighthouse audit, does not run a service worker, and cannot see a criterion browsers might add in the future. A clean report describes what these checks found, not a guarantee every browser will prompt to install.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace testing the actual install prompt in a real browser. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use it as a system of record.

Nothing leaves your browser. The CLI's requests go straight from your machine to the URL you name (and whatever that page's own manifest and icons point at) -- never through this site. The page you're reading now only parses JSON you paste into it locally; nothing is uploaded. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day -- no target URLs, no manifest contents, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

vs-lighthouse.html.text:
← PWA Installability Checker

This checker vs. Lighthouse

Lighthouse is Google's open-source auditing tool for web pages, built into Chrome DevTools and also runnable from the command line, as an npm package, or through PageSpeed Insights. Point it at a URL and it drives a real Chrome (or Chromium) instance to score the page across several categories -- performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO, and, among its PWA-related audits, installable-manifest: the same manifest, name, display-mode, secure-origin, and icon checks this tool runs. Lighthouse's own documentation on web.dev describes that audit in detail.

That is a much broader tool doing a much broader job, and it needs a browser to do it: Lighthouse launches Chrome (via chrome-launcher or Puppeteer) to render the page before it can audit anything, which means a Chrome or Chromium binary has to exist on whatever machine runs it. This checker does one narrower thing without that dependency. It is a zero-dependency Node command that fetches your page's HTML, the <link rel="manifest"> it points at, the manifest JSON, and every icon the manifest lists, using plain HTTP requests -- no browser, no rendering, no screenshot. It classifies the result against the documented installability criteria and stops there. It has no performance timing, no accessibility rules, and no SEO score.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Get a full picture of a page -- performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO, and PWA checks together, rendered the way a visitor's browser sees it. Lighthouse -- this checker only ever answers the installability question.
Find out whether a page's manifest and icons clear Chrome's documented installability criteria, without installing or launching a browser. This checker -- one Node command, plain HTTP requests, a plain-English report.
Gate a deploy in CI on a manifest regression, on a runner image with no Chrome and no Puppeteer download budget. This checker -- zero dependencies beyond Node, and it never launches a browser.
Audit rendered performance, layout shift, or real accessibility violations that only show up once the page runs. Lighthouse -- this checker never renders the page, so it cannot see anything that depends on rendering.
See the install prompt fire in an actual browser session, or capture a full audit report with scores and a trace. Lighthouse (or Chrome DevTools' own Lighthouse panel) -- this checker only classifies a probe's JSON output, never a live page.

These compose rather than compete. A reasonable setup runs this checker on every commit that touches a manifest or an icon asset -- cheap, no browser, fails fast and names the exact field -- and keeps a full Lighthouse run for the broader audit that only a rendered page can answer. Neither one replaces the other.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Lighthouse?

Reach for Lighthouse when you want the full picture: performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO, and PWA installability scored together against a page you name, using a real Chrome instance driving the page the way a visitor's browser would. Reach for this checker when you only want the installability question answered -- manifest present and parseable, a name, an installable display mode, a secure origin, a reachable icon -- without installing or launching Chrome at all, for example on a CI runner with no browser image or on a machine where Puppeteer's download is unwelcome.

Lighthouse is free too. What does this add?

Being free is not the difference -- Lighthouse is Google's open-source project under an Apache-2.0 licence, and running it costs nothing. What differs is the dependency and the scope. Lighthouse drives a real Chrome or Chromium instance (via chrome-launcher or Puppeteer) to produce its report, which is a real download and a real browser process to keep current. This checker is a zero-dependency Node script: it fetches your page's HTML, its manifest, and its icons with plain HTTP requests, classifies the result against the same documented installability criteria, and needs nothing beyond Node itself. It also does only that one job -- it has no performance, accessibility, or SEO score to produce or to keep out of your way.

Does this replace running Lighthouse?

No. Lighthouse's installable-manifest audit is one line item inside a much larger report, and that larger report is doing real work this checker does not attempt -- performance timing, accessibility rules, and the rest of Lighthouse's PWA and best-practices checks, all measured against a page rendered in an actual browser. This checker reads the same manifest and icon criteria Lighthouse's own documentation describes and reports on nothing else. Run Lighthouse for the full audit; run this when installability is the one question and a browser is the one thing you would rather not install.

Is this page affiliated with Google or Lighthouse?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Google, and Lighthouse and Chrome are trademarks of Google LLC, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. The description of Lighthouse and its installable-manifest audit on this page is drawn from Google's own public documentation; check web.dev and the Lighthouse repository for what the current release covers.

vs-reading-the-manifest-by-eye.html.text:
← PWA Installability Checker

This checker vs. reading manifest.json by eye

The free way to check installability is to open manifest.json in an editor or a browser tab and read it: is there a name, does display look right, are the icons roughly the expected sizes. That catches the obviously broken cases -- an empty file, a display value that is plainly wrong -- and costs nothing but a minute of attention.

This checker runs the same documented criteria Chrome uses, but does two things a read-through has no easy way to do. First, it actually fetches every icon the manifest lists and confirms each one responds successfully as an image, rather than trusting that a path which looks right in the JSON also resolves on the live site. Second, it resolves every field to its spec default before judging it -- an absent display is not "nothing to check", it is the spec's own default of "browser", which fails the install criteria outright.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Spot-check a manifest you just hand-wrote for an obviously missing field before committing. Reading it by eye -- fast, and good enough to catch a typo or a blank file.
Confirm every icon a manifest lists actually loads, at the right size, with an image content type -- not just that the path looks plausible. This checker -- it fetches each icon and checks the response, which a read-through of the JSON cannot do at all.
Know whether a manifest with no display field passes or fails, without having to remember the spec's default. This checker -- it resolves the absence to "browser" and reports the fail, the same way Chrome does.
Parse a sizes attribute that lists several tokens on one icon entry and confirm at least one clears 192px. This checker -- it parses every token rather than relying on a glance at the first one.
Check whether the page itself is served over a secure origin, which the manifest file itself says nothing about. This checker -- it checks the page's own scheme, a fact the manifest JSON cannot contain.
Gate a CI run on a manifest regression without opening a file in an editor at all. This checker -- one Node command, a machine-checkable pass/fail.

A quick read of the file is a reasonable first pass while you are still writing the manifest. This checker is what you run before you trust that pass -- it fetches what the manifest points at instead of assuming the paths resolve, and it applies the spec's defaults instead of relying on a reader to recall them.

Common questions

Isn't just opening manifest.json and reading it enough?

For the fields that are obviously wrong on sight -- no name field at all, display set to something that is clearly not standalone -- yes. What a read-through cannot do without extra steps is confirm each listed icon URL actually resolves to a reachable image of the right size, or remember that a missing display field is not neutral: the spec's own default for an absent display is "browser", which Chrome's installability criteria explicitly exclude. A quick read tends to skip past an absent field as "nothing to flag" rather than resolving it to the value it defaults to.

What does eyeballing the manifest miss that this checker catches?

Three things in particular. First, icon reachability: a manifest can list a 192x192 icon path that looks correct in the JSON and still 404, get served with the wrong content type, or point at a build artifact nobody committed -- none of that is visible from the manifest file alone, only from actually fetching it. Second, the sizes attribute can carry several space-separated size tokens on one icon entry ("48x48 96x96 192x192"), and confirming at least one clears the 192px minimum means parsing every token, not just glancing at the first one. Third, the secure-origin requirement depends on how the page itself was served, which manifest.json says nothing about at all.

Why does a missing display field count as a hard fail here?

Because the Web App Manifest spec's own default for an absent "display" is "browser", and Chrome's installability criteria explicitly exclude "browser" from the modes it will install. A human reading the file sees no display key and often reads that as "not set, move on" -- but the browser resolves the absence to a concrete value that fails the check. This tool applies that same resolution automatically instead of relying on the reader to remember the spec's default.

Is anything I paste into either process uploaded?

There is nothing to upload either way. Reading manifest.json in an editor or browser tab involves no third party at all, and this checker's browser page only renders a report from JSON you paste in locally -- the CLI that actually fetches the page, manifest, and icons talks directly to the URL you name, never through this site.
